turnPlan.subject: physics
turnPlan.question: what is a parallel circuit

qualitativeClaims.claim: A parallel circuit is an electrical circuit where components are connected across the same two points, creating multiple paths for current to flow.
qualitativeClaims.expected: Components share the same voltage across them.

qualitativeClaims.claim: In a parallel circuit, the total current is the sum of the currents through each branch.
The voltage across each component in a parallel circuit is identical.
The total resistance in a parallel circuit is less than the smallest individual resistance.
If one branch of a parallel circuit is broken, current can still flow through the other branches.

assumptions: Components are ideal (no internal resistance).
The circuit is connected to a constant voltage source.

givens.sourceText: time on rough incline is 50% more than on smooth

qualitativeClaims.claim: Smooth-incline acceleration along the slope
Rough-incline acceleration with kinetic friction
Equal slide length from rest gives t = √(2L/a), so t_r/t_s = √(a_s/a_r) = 3/2, hence a_r/a_s = 4/9
Result matches the listed option 5/9

g cancels in the ratio

turnPlan.subject: physics
turnPlan.question: what is a parallel circuit

qualitativeClaims.claim: A parallel circuit is an electrical circuit in which two or more components are connected across the same two nodes, forming multiple branches so current has more than one path.
qualitativeClaims.expected: definition: components share the same two endpoints; multiple current paths

qualitativeClaims.claim: The voltage across every branch of a parallel circuit is the same.
The total current from the source equals the sum of the branch currents (Kirchhoff's current law).
The equivalent resistance of parallel resistors is found from the reciprocal sum, and is always less than the smallest branch resistance.
If one branch of a parallel circuit is broken or switched off, the other branches keep working because each has its own complete path.
qualitativeClaims.expected: independent branch operation; contrast with series circuit

qualitativeClaims.claim: Everyday example: household outlets and lights are wired in parallel so each appliance gets full mains voltage and can be switched independently.

assumptions: Ideal wires and sources (negligible internal resistance) for the stated relations
Components compared are passive resistive branches
A verified illustration is required by the question's spatial or explicit visual request.

items.question: what is a parallel circuit

turnPlan.subject: physics
turnPlan.question: what is a parallel circuit

qualitativeClaims.claim: A parallel circuit is an electrical circuit in which two or more components are connected across the same two nodes, forming multiple branches so current has more than one path.
qualitativeClaims.expected: definition: components share the same two endpoints; multiple current paths

qualitativeClaims.claim: The voltage across every branch of a parallel circuit is the same.
The total current from the source equals the sum of the branch currents (Kirchhoff's current law).
The equivalent resistance of parallel resistors is found from the reciprocal sum, and is always less than the smallest branch resistance.
If one branch of a parallel circuit is broken or switched off, the other branches keep working because each has its own complete path.
qualitativeClaims.expected: independent branch operation; contrast with series circuit

qualitativeClaims.claim: Everyday example: household outlets and lights are wired in parallel so each appliance gets full mains voltage and can be switched independently.

assumptions: Ideal wires and sources (negligible internal resistance) for the stated relations
Components compared are passive resistive branches

turnPlan.question: A 2.0 kg block on frictionless ice already moves at 4.0 m/s. No horizontal force acts. Find the velocity after 5.0 s, and explain using Newton’s first law why you must not write v = u + at with a = g. Then contrast with the same block on a rough floor with μ_k = 0.10, g = 10 m/s^2, which does slow down.

derived.sourceText: block stops at t = 4.0 s < 5.0 s, so v = 0

qualitativeClaims.claim: On frictionless ice, no horizontal force acts, so by Newton's first law the velocity stays constant at 4.0 m/s for all t, including t = 5.0 s.

Writing v = u + at with a = g is wrong here: g is the free-fall acceleration due to gravity, which acts only vertically. On ice the vertical forces (weight and normal) cancel and horizontal acceleration is zero, so a ≠ g horizontally.
Newton's first law: an object in motion continues at constant velocity unless a net external force acts; frictionless ice provides no net horizontal force, so no acceleration.
On the rough floor, kinetic friction f = μ_k N = μ_k m g opposes motion, giving horizontal acceleration a = -μ_k g = -1.0 m/s² (deceleration).

Naively v = u + at gives -1.0 m/s at t = 5.0 s, but kinetic friction cannot reverse the motion; the block stops at t_stop = u/(μ_k g) = 4.0 s and then remains at rest, so the physical answer is v = 0 at t = 5.0 s.
qualitativeClaims.expected: v_rough(5 s) = 0 m/s because t_stop = 4.0 s < 5.0 s

qualitativeClaims.claim: Contrast: frictionless case has a = 0 and v constant; rough case has a = -μ_k g until stopping, showing that v = u + at applies only while the assumed force (kinetic friction) actually acts.
qualitativeClaims.expected: ice: v = 4.0 m/s; rough: v = 0 m/s at 5.0 s

assumptions: Ice is perfectly frictionless, so horizontal net force is zero.
Vertical forces (weight, normal) cancel on the horizontal surface in both cases.
On the rough floor, kinetic friction with constant μ_k acts while the block slides.
Once the block stops on the rough floor, it stays at rest (static friction holds it; no driving force).
Motion is one-dimensional along the initial velocity direction.

Find the velocity after 5.0 s, and explain using Newton’s first law why you must not write v = u + at with a = g. Then contrast with the same block on a rough floor with μ_k = 0.10, g = 10 m/s^2, which does slow down.

turnPlan.question: A 2.0 kg block on frictionless ice already moves at 4.0 m/s. No horizontal force acts. Find the velocity after 5.0 s, and explain using Newton’s first law why you must not write v = u + at with a = g. Then contrast with the same block on a rough floor with μ_k = 0.10, g = 10 m/s^2, which does slow down.

derived.sourceText: block stops at t = 4.0 s < 5.0 s, so v = 0

qualitativeClaims.claim: On frictionless ice, no horizontal force acts, so by Newton's first law the velocity stays constant at 4.0 m/s for all t, including t = 5.0 s.

Writing v = u + at with a = g is wrong here: g is the free-fall acceleration due to gravity, which acts only vertically. On ice the vertical forces (weight and normal) cancel and horizontal acceleration is zero, so a ≠ g horizontally.
Newton's first law: an object in motion continues at constant velocity unless a net external force acts; frictionless ice provides no net horizontal force, so no acceleration.
On the rough floor, kinetic friction f = μ_k N = μ_k m g opposes motion, giving horizontal acceleration a = -μ_k g = -1.0 m/s² (deceleration).

Naively v = u + at gives -1.0 m/s at t = 5.0 s, but kinetic friction cannot reverse the motion; the block stops at t_stop = u/(μ_k g) = 4.0 s and then remains at rest, so the physical answer is v = 0 at t = 5.0 s.
qualitativeClaims.expected: v_rough(5 s) = 0 m/s because t_stop = 4.0 s < 5.0 s

qualitativeClaims.claim: Contrast: frictionless case has a = 0 and v constant; rough case has a = -μ_k g until stopping, showing that v = u + at applies only while the assumed force (kinetic friction) actually acts.
qualitativeClaims.expected: ice: v = 4.0 m/s; rough: v = 0 m/s at 5.0 s

assumptions: Ice is perfectly frictionless, so horizontal net force is zero.
Vertical forces (weight, normal) cancel on the horizontal surface in both cases.
On the rough floor, kinetic friction with constant μ_k acts while the block slides.
Once the block stops on the rough floor, it stays at rest (static friction holds it; no driving force).
Motion is one-dimensional along the initial velocity direction.
